description: We are a team of three from Chiclayo, Peru, working on the Field Shift challenge. We built AgroShift, an open-source, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that uses NASA satellite data (POWER, SMAP, GLDAS, FIRMS) to help small farmers in Lambayeque anticipate water stress and adapt their crops to climate variability. Our skills: web development, data integration and accessibility. We welcome collaborators with agronomy or remote-sensing experience.
summary: AgroShift is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that helps small and medium farmers decide what to plant next. In five short questions, the farmer gives a location (or marks a four-corner parcel on satellite imagery), current crop, goal, available water and planting date. AgroShift fuses four NASA sources (POWER weather, SMAP soil moisture, GLDAS temperature trends via Giovanni, and FIRMS active-fire detections) with FAO ECOCROP crop rules, then shows Plan A and a drier-scenario Plan B side by side. This answers Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data by turning satellite evidence into practical choices that save water, protect soil through rotation and warn early about heat and fires. Every statement traces to a dataset or documented rule; AI never writes agronomic advice. Built for low-cost phones, weak connectivity and users with no technical background, it loads in about 55 KiB and works offline, so farmers in remote areas can still decide with confidence.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

AgroShift helps a small or medium farmer decide what to plant next. A five-question quiz (location, current or last crop, goal, available water, planting date) leads to two options shown side by side: Plan A (main plan) and Plan B (contingency for a drier, water-limited scenario). Instead of typing coordinates, the farmer can mark the four corners of a plot on a satellite map (Esri World Imagery); the app computes the centroid and the area in hectares and queries data for that exact spot.

The data layer fuses four NASA sources: NASA POWER (temperature, rainfall, humidity, solar radiation), NASA SMAP L4 soil moisture (surface and root zone, via AppEEARS), NASA Giovanni with GLDAS (air-temperature anomaly and trend) and NASA FIRMS (nearby active-fire detections). A deterministic engine applies FAO ECOCROP crop requirements plus rotation, thermal and rainfall rules, and returns reasons, restrictions, actions and "what to check" for each plan. Every statement is traceable to a dataset or a documented rule, with value, unit, period, grid and limits. Hypothetical scenarios are labelled "Assumption: not a forecast", and missing data is shown as unavailable instead of a false alarm.

An optional explanation feature uses Amazon Bedrock only to SELECT which engine-produced facts answer the farmer's question; the visible sentence always comes from fixed templates, so the model cannot invent claims or hallucinate advice.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Water savings: the farmer sees how the crop choice and planting date fit rainfall and soil moisture, and gets a drier-scenario Plan B before the season starts.

- Soil protection: rotation rules avoid planting the same crop family back to back.

- Early warning: heat-trend and nearby-fire alerts based on NASA data.

- Access: free, no sign-up, English and Spanish, large touch targets, and built for low-cost phones and weak connectivity. The goal is to bring NASA Earth observation to farmers who cannot read raw satellite data.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Astro, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, Leaflet (Esri World Imagery tiles), Supabase PostgreSQL with Row Level Security (shared cache and request budget), Vercel (hosting), Amazon Bedrock (fact selection), Vitest (384 passing unit tests), Playwright (20 end-to-end tests), and Python python-pptx (pitch deck). Data: NASA POWER, SMAP, Giovanni/GLDAS, FIRMS, FAO ECOCROP, Open-Meteo Geocoding (GeoNames). No special hardware is required; it runs in any modern phone browser.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Hybrid architecture: a deterministic, versioned rules engine makes every recommendation; AI is limited to choosing fact keys (JSON, temperature 0) and never writes agronomic advice. If Bedrock is unavailable or returns invalid output, the app falls back to local template answers.

- Ultralight: the initial page weighs 55.45 KiB gzipped.

- Offline-first: a Service Worker caches pages, scripts and bundled NASA snapshots (Peru, India, Kenya), so the plan can be computed on the device on slow 2G/3G rural networks or with no network.

- Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA target with AAA contrast for main text, 48 px touch targets, keyboard use, reduced-motion and forced-colors support, and status shown with symbol, text and border.

- Honesty about uncertainty, privacy (farm locations are not sent to Bedrock), and open source under Apache 2.0.
